item.text: The Crime and Corruption Commission commissioned research on Queensland public sector employees’ corruption perceptions to monitor prevention work and guide planning.
item.support:
so the CCC can 
monitor the impact of its prevention agenda and 
inform future strategic planning.

item.text: An online survey collected 5,957 completed responses between 28 March and 9 May 2025 from state government and hospital and health service employees.
item.support:
An online survey of Queensland public sector employees was 
conducted between 28 March and 9 May 2025.

item.text: The CCC reported that employees ranked policy non-compliance, mishandling confidential information, and bullying and harassment among the highest workplace corruption risks.
item.support:
The 
behaviours considered the highest risk included non-
compliance with policies and procedures, mishandling 
of confidential information and bullying and 
harassment

item.text: The CCC reported that 55% said they had witnessed or suspected corruption in the preceding five years, and 55% of that group had not reported it.
item.support:
Over half (55%) of public sector employees have either witnessed, or 
think they have witnessed, corruption in the past 5 years.

item.text: The CCC reported that 72% would report corruption, but only 33% expected meaningful action and 52% expected personal repercussions.
item.support:
However, half of respondents (52%) 
expect they would experience personal 
repercussions if they  reported corruption

item.quote:
Public sector employees are more likely to feel comfortable lodging 
a complaint with the CCC than they are lodging a complaint within 
their workplace.

There is some scepticism around the outcomes 
of reporting corruption; one in three agree 
meaningful action would be taken (33%), but 
similar proportions disagree (36%).
